rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sarah’s wonder sought assurance that the apparent obstacle to the promised tidings would be overcome.
rows.anchor: the apparent hindrance to the fulfilment of these tidings would be surmounted

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The angels understood Sarah’s laughter and words, then respectfully reminded her of her standing as a prophet’s wife.
rows.anchor: they fully understood the reason for Sarah’s laughter and the sentence she uttered

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The masculine plural pronoun used to address Sarah politely addresses the women of a household and conveys modesty and respect.
rows.anchor: In Arabic, this is a very civilized and polite way of addressing women of a household.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur’anic address to the Prophet’s household is cited as another example of the respectful masculine plural form.
rows.anchor: Women of the Prophet’s House! God seeks only to eradicate filth from you and to fully purify you.

rows.speaker: Imr’u al-Qays
rows.claim: The cited line from Imr’u al-Qays supplies a classical Arabic parallel for the household-address style.
rows.anchor: Imr’u al-Qays has said:69 ﻓﻠﻮ أن أﻫﻞ

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The construction suppresses an incomplete verb before yujadiluna, understood as sara; the same ellipsis occurs at 11:38.
rows.anchor: Several examples of this suppression have been pointed out in this exegesis.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abraham’s argument is deferential but emphatic persuasion; before learning the angels’ mission, he remained hesitant and worried.
rows.anchor: The argument of Abraham (sws) alluded to here is one which is friendly and respectful

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After receiving the son’s glad tidings and becoming settled about his own situation, Abraham turned his concern to Lot’s people and pleaded for them.
rows.anchor: as soon as he received glad tidings of a son and was at peace with his own situation, he started worrying about the nation of Lot

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Genesis account of Abraham repeatedly bargaining down the number of righteous people whom God would require to spare Sodom illustrates the form of pleading the author says God likes.
rows.anchor: Then Abraham approached him and said: “Will you sweep away the righteous with the wicked?

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abraham’s love, trust, concern, and kindness in pleading for Lot’s people are beyond words, and God praised him for them.
rows.anchor: Abraham’s love and trust for his Lord found in this passage as well as his concern and kindness are beyond words.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The word awwāh is an intensive form associated with repeated sighing and denotes a deeply sympathetic, caring, kind-hearted person.
rows.anchor: In other words, it refers to a person who is very sympathetic, caring and kind-hearted.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abraham’s compassion is shown by his continued intercession for Lot’s vile people even though their punishment was imminent.
rows.anchor: Abraham’s benevolence and compassion are beyond any doubt if he can argue with God to spare such a nasty and wretched nation

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God praised Abraham’s compassion and plea but told him the time for intercession had ended and the punishment was now due.
rows.anchor: He has also informed him that the time of prayer and commendation has expired.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The punishment cannot be postponed after warning and is decisive; nobody can ward it off because no one can challenge God’s directive.
rows.anchor: none has the might to take on God’s directive.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Lot’s distress arose because the handsome male guests at his door invited the attention of his immoral people.
rows.anchor: handsome boys coming to his door was a plain invitation to the scoundrels of his nation.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Lot’s offer of his daughters was not an actual choice; it was an anxious final appeal meant to awaken conscience by showing his concern for his guests’ integrity.
rows.anchor: Presenting his daughters was not a choice given by Lot (sws) to his nation.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: By offering his closest relatives for the guests’ protection, Lot tried to make the people recognize their blindness and the indecency of their assault.
rows.anchor: he was willing to go as far as to sacrifice his closest of relatives for them.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Lot’s final question about whether any sensible person remained should have stirred even a little honor; their failure to respond showed they lacked decency and humanity.
rows.anchor: when after this also their conscience was not awakened, it clearly meant that they had no element of decency and humanity left in them.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The people meant that Lot should stop obstructing them and let them do as they wished.
rows.anchor: They meant that Lot (sws) should not needlessly create impediments in their way. He should let them do what they want to.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Lot spoke in acute anxiety after losing hope in his people, using a cultural norm to make a conclusive appeal: granting refuge to a calamity-stricken seeker was virtuous, while refusing was mean.
rows.anchor: Arabia of those times giving refuge to someone struck by a calamity when he was seeking refuge was considered a great virtue.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After Lot’s appeal, the angels disclosed their identity and instructed him about what to do next.
rows.anchor: Once Lot (sws) said the words cited earlier, the angels revealed their true identity and advised him what to do next.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sijjīl is an Arabicized form of the Persian sang-i gil.
rows.anchor: The word sijjīl is the Arabicised form of the Persian word sang-i gil.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One reading takes the stones as already under the wrongdoers’ feet, lifted by the furious wind and showered onto their heads.
rows.anchor: the furious wind sent by God picked them up from below the feet of these wretched people and showered them on their heads.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alternatively, the pronoun may refer to Lot’s settlement and the unjust to Quraysh: the nearby ruins lay on their route to Syria and should teach them.
rows.anchor: Another option is to regard the antecedent of the pronoun

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author develops the alternative reading that Lot’s settlement was near Quraysh and its travelers to Syria should learn from its fate.
rows.anchor: In verse 89 ahead, Shu‘ayb (sws) while addressing his nation has said

rows.speaker: Ust āz Farāhī
rows.claim: Farāhī’s summary describes a blizzard that hardened into a stone storm, first pelting people and then razing their houses under windblown sand and pebbles.
rows.anchor: Following is a summary of what Ust āz Farāhī has written regarding the nature of punishment meted out to the nation of Lot

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The messengers’ mission from within their people conclusively communicates the truth; monotheism is the center of their preaching, and deviation from it opens further error.
rows.anchor: monotheism occupies the centre of gravity and the focal point in the preaching of God’s messengers.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Madyan’s people were prosperous traders whose characteristic moral corruption was dishonest weighing and measuring, treated as a professional skill leading to social anarchy.
rows.anchor: dishonesty in weighing and measuring became their skill and profession.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Shu’ayb begins with worship of God alone and calls the traders to reform; prosperity obliges gratitude and obedience, while ingratitude turns luxury into destruction.
rows.anchor: The very purpose of God in granting such wealth and riches to a nation is to see if it shows gratitude and obedience to Him or not.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Shu’ayb warns that if they do not reform, punishment will suddenly surround them and none will escape.
rows.anchor: If it is ungrateful and disobedient, then this very life of opulence and luxury becomes a means of its destruction.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: People should make earthly life reflect goodness, justice, and knowledge rather than disorder; God gives such people respite only to a limit before wiping out miscreants.
rows.anchor: their life on earth should reflect goodness, justice and knowledge instead of creating anarchy and disorder in it.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Baqiyyatullah means legitimate profit: honest earnings may be smaller but are superior because they are blessed in this world and the next, while fraud profits are condemned and become fire in the next life.
rows.anchor: If a trader weighs and measures with honesty, abstains from deception and other such ill-ways

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Shu’ayb’s duty is to explain right and wrong fully; the people bear the consequences of their response, while he is a warner and bearer of glad tidings, not their keeper.
rows.anchor: he has fully explained the right and the wrong to his nation.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The people mock Shu’ayb’s prayer as if it required abandoning ancestral worship and forbade using their wealth as they pleased; they sarcastically call him the only wise man.
rows.anchor: Does your prayer teach you that we leave those which our forefathers used to worship or we should not use our wealth the way we want to?

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Bayyina means an innate conviction and belief from God that guides a person, provided bad company has not distorted his nature.
rows.anchor: It refers to the conviction and belief innately found in a person from God.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The goodly provision granted to Shu’ayb is revelation, parallel to the way material sustenance supports the body and revelation sustains the spirit.
rows.anchor: divine revelation is need for sustaining his spiritual being.

rows.speaker: Jesus
rows.claim: Jesus is reported as saying that people need God’s word as well as physical bread.
rows.anchor: Jesus (sws) is reported to have said: “Man shall not live on bread alone, but on every word that comes from the mouth of God.”

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The conditional clause’s answer is omitted and supplied from 11:63: if Shu’ayb has clear evidence and revelation, deviation would leave him without rescue from divine wrath.
rows.anchor: The answer to the conditional clause in the first part of the verse is suppressed.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Shu’ayb’s call arose from his heart even before revelation, and revelation later substantiated it; the mockery falsely treats his earnest preaching as contrived.
rows.anchor: what he has said to them was the call of his heart even before he received divine revelation

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Shu’ayb denies that he is stopping dishonest trade to monopolize the market; opponents may have spread that allegation because he had a small business.
rows.anchor: his purpose was to make them honest while he himself takes control of the market

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He wants only to reform matters as far as possible and relies on God’s grace, trust, and turning to Him for help.
rows.anchor: he only wants to mend affairs as far as he could.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Shiqāq means stubbornness and opposition.
rows.anchor: means “stubbornness and opposition.” It may be kept in mind

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Because Lot’s people lived close in time and place, Shu’ayb says their fate is recent nearby testimony, not a remote tale, of the wrath invited by opposition.
rows.anchor: both the period and location of the nation of Lot (sws) were close to those of Shu‘ayb (sws).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Turning to God means abandoning present conduct and adopting the way God approves.
rows.anchor: The words “turn towards Him” means that they should give up their present behaviour

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Repentance has two required elements, seeking forgiveness and reforming one’s conduct; without both, it is not accepted.
rows.anchor: repentance has two components: seeking forgiveness and mending ways.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The divine attributes of mercy and love both urge the people to seek forgiveness and subtly promise that sincere repentance, however grave the sin, will be accepted.
rows.anchor: if they sincerely repent, they will not find God rejecting their request.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The people dismiss Shu’ayb’s message as far-fetched, claim they would otherwise be receptive, then threaten him; they fear his clan, not Shu’ayb individually.
rows.anchor: baseless and far-fetched is Shu‘ayb’s (sws) message to them

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: They specially threatened to stone Shu’ayb because he disparaged their deities; Abraham and other prophets received the same threat for that reason.
rows.anchor: Shu‘ayb (sws) was specially threatened of being stoned to death because he used to disparage their deities.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Shu’ayb’s question about whether his clan is more powerful than God expresses his trust in God.
rows.anchor: These words of Shu‘ayb’s (sws) reflect his trust in God.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The word murtaqab means a place.
rows.anchor: The word ٌﻣ means “place.”

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Shu’ayb will continue warning and giving glad tidings despite opposition; he cannot predict when punishment will arrive, but its signs are present and he awaits it.
rows.anchor: he would continue with his mission of delivering warnings and glad tidings to them even if they continue to do whatever they want

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The account of Madyan’s punishment here repeats material already treated at 11:66–68.
rows.anchor: The content of these verses has already been brought up in verses 66-68 earlier.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Moses and Pharaoh account is brief here, whereas the preceding sūrah Yūnus gave it in detail and only briefly mentioned other prophets; the reversal makes the paired sūrahs complement one another.
rows.anchor: In this way both these sūrahs complement one another and thus follow the pattern of paired occurrence of sūrahs.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Signs refers to Moses’ recurring general signs, while the clear proof is the special staff miracle that gave him dominance over Pharaoh and his courtiers.
rows.anchor: The word “signs” refers to all those general signs that appeared from Moses (sws) every now and then.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The staff miracle is called a clear proof because it was a forceful argument that damaged Pharaoh and his courtiers’ standing before their people.
rows.anchor: the special sign which gave Moses (sws) clear dominance over the Pharaoh and his courtiers

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Egyptians followed Pharaoh instead of God’s messenger and were doomed, as followers of such leaders generally are.
rows.anchor: these wretched people followed the Pharaoh and were doomed.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Warada means to step beside a spring to drink; Pharaoh will lead his followers to Hell’s seething spring, the worst destination.
rows.anchor: The verb وردmeans to step beside a spring to drink water.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The final section recalls what the past accounts were meant to teach Quraysh and what guidance Muhammad and his followers can draw from them.
rows.anchor: In them, attention is directed to the facts found in the past anecdotes and to highlight which they were actually narrated to the addressees.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Verse 120 fully explains the point made in verse 100.
rows.anchor: Verse 120 ahead fully explains what is stated here.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Hasid literally refers to a harvested crop and here denotes settlements entirely destroyed by divine punishment.
rows.anchor: Here it refers to the settlements which were totally destroyed by divine punishment.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Egypt exemplifies a settlement that remained standing after God removed its inhabitants by drowning Pharaoh and his people.
rows.anchor: Houses remained intact while their inhabitants were wiped out.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The term also refers to the destroyed settlements of the peoples of Hud and Lot.
rows.anchor: of the nation of H ūd (sws) and Lot (sws).
